segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Freddie is the general manager of a car dealership these days, but he used to be a car salesman. And he was a good one, partly because he's got what he calls the gift for the gab. His go-to move in lots of situations is to finish his sentence and then laugh, even when the sentence is bad news. Like, here he is assessing his chances of making his sales goal for the month.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I'll give it a 50/50 right now because it's early.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Or this is him talking about a month when the car dealership did not make its sales goal.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: And I'm strictly commission, so I make nothing.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So when Freddie is not laughing, you know it's bad. In mid-October, Freddie did not laugh much at his weekly meetings with the guys who sell cars for him.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: All right. Good morning. All right. In the beginning of the month, I went through the room and I told everybody where they had to be. Jason, you have 16 cars out. You need 10 more for the month for 26. I want to see you there.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Bob Lundy, you have six out. You need nine more. Scotty, you're at 10 right now. You need to be at 18.

segments.text: Last month, they didn't make their sales goal. That was September. The first week of school is always bad for car sales in the suburbs. They were supposed to sell 127 cars and trucks. They sold 82. So they have to make October.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when I say have to make, this is not some sort of abstract, feel-good, "compete with the dealership down the block just for fun" kind of competition. They're part of Chrysler. And if they sell 129 cars and trucks by the end of October, Chrysler will pay them a bonus that's pretty much the difference between the dealership being in the black or being in the red for the month, somewhere between $65,000 and $85,000, depending on which models they sell. Different cars earn different amounts. If they sell 128 cars, fall just one car short, they get nothing.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: That's the worksheet that Chrysler sends us to show us what money we can earn by how many cars we sell.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And there's a new one every month?

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: Every month.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the middle of the month, the owner of this dealership, a sweet-faced guy named Marc Brodlieb, and Freddie, show me the document where Chrysler set their October sales goal.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: No. No. This changes every month.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: At their whim.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: At their whim.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: And that's another frustration. We have no idea what the number's going to be and really how they compute it. We've had numbers as high as 159. And we fight and we go crazy. It's cockamamie, if anyone knows what that means.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because basically they shift around the ground rules on you.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: Every month.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What makes this tricky is that there are four other Jeep dealerships within 10 miles of Marc and Freddie, and Marc says that most customers will shop price at two or three of them. So to stay competitive, Marc and Freddie do what pretty much everybody else does. They set lower prices, knock hundreds of dollars off the price of the cars, sometimes sell them for less than they pay Chrysler for them, with the hope that they're going to hit their sales goal and get the bonus to make up the difference.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: But there's no guarantee we will hit this number. So the pressure is huge because we have already given away the money to the consumer, using that to sell the car.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: So I need a big day today. I need a big day, no bull. I really need a big day today.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So with 12 days left to go in the month, numbers wobbly, Freddie laid it on thick during his weekly meeting with the sales team. He told them he sees them over the dealership's security cams.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I look through the video. I watch you guys in there. All on your computers, going to different websites, chilling. Dude, get on higher gear. This is no joke. I've got to be at that number, or I'm telling you, I'm not going to be a nice guy. So put your nose right to the ground and come out shooting today, everybody.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I want balloons in all the departments. I want the radios down on. Put the convertible tops down all over the place. I want tons of balloons in the showroom. I just don't want one balloon to a car. Balloon the whole freaking place so it looks like a circus.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Make it seem like we're having a monster sale and it's a party, because we've got to be at the big number by the 31st, midnight, period, no ands, ifs, and buts.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So everybody grabs balloons. Grown men inflate and tie and decorate. It's a truism in their business, balloons sell cars. And then nobody shows up for an hour, two hours, three hours-- four hours. Saturday should be one of their busiest days, and it's empty.

segments.text: Hey, Freddie. How's it going today so far?

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Shit. Really bad. Really slow. Really, really slow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Early afternoon, Freddie told one of our producers, Brian Reed, that it was way slower than usual. I don't know if you can catch this, but try to notice the song that is playing over the radio in the background as they talk.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What do you think it is? What's going on?

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Not a clue. With all the advertisings out there and everything else, we should be swamped. I'm stressing. Oh, I'm stressing.

segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.text: [MUSIC - "DON'T WORRY BE HAPPY" BY BOBBY MCFERRIN]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Marc, who owns this dealership, and Freddie, who runs it, both know that most people do not trust car dealers. Most people think that they're ripping us off, throwing on extra charges, milking us for every dime. And they say, if you and I only knew the reality, we would see that, in fact, the dealer is not making a killing off us. In fact, the dealer is often squeaking by with a very thin profit margin. They say it is all very different from what people think. And to prove their point, they let us watch.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A bunch of us from our radio show, we recorded them as they headed towards the end of the month, trying to make their goal, trying to sell 129 cars, which, you know, you would think that would be very straightforward, very businesslike. After all, new cars and trucks, they're 15% of all retail sales. But if what we saw was typical, what that means is that hundreds of billions of dollars in economic activity and nearly 2 million jobs exist thanks only to millions of messy seat-of-the-pants deals, many of which barely come together, as salesmen sweat out their end-of-the-month quotas. It is way more chaotic than we expected.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And we saw things, it's true, we think will surprise a lot of car buyers. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. Today, one car dealership tries to sell 129 cars. We get to know the resolute men and women who try to pull that off.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Quick note, this show is a rerun. Everything you'll hear in this hour all happened in October a couple years back. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I wish I could pretend that we got interested in this subject at our radio show because we realized what an important part of the economy car sales are. And I wish I could pretend that we did a huge survey to find the most typical dealership out there. But in fact, we got interested in this topic and this particular dealership-- Town & Country Jeep Chrysler Dodge Ram is what it's called, in Levittown, New York, on Long Island-- when one of our coworkers here at the radio show, Robyn Semien, bought a used car there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here's how that happened. A friend of hers who knows all about cars told her that the only vehicle that she should even consider for her young family is the Honda Pilot. So she went looking online. She saw one listed on cars.com. It was at Town & Country.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she called. And she had no intention at all of going to look at the car. But a salesman convinced her, oh, you know what? You should come out today, right today. Talked her into it, which meant an hour-long ride on a train from Brooklyn with her husband and her four-year-old.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then once she got there, they upsold her to a newer, more expensive vehicle, a Jeep Liberty, which she drove off the lot 24 hours later. Robyn told me this story in the car in question on our first ride out to the dealership.

segments.speaker: Robyn Semien
segments.text: Yeah. I mean, the Honda Pilot, I think, is across the board, less problems, lasts longer, better gas mileage.

segments.speaker: Robyn Semien
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Robyn Semien
segments.text: I know. I know. I know. I know, but I love this car.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You got that? These people are such good salesmen, not only did she pay more, not only did they put her into a Jeep, which meant that, since they are a Jeep dealer, they could sell her a warranty, which they also did for a few thousand dollars, she came out of this loving her car and loving them. How did they do this?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, before we go any further, I think I should give you a quick primer on the basic setup and cast of characters at this dealership. New cars are sold at Town & Country-- and we're going to be spending most of our time with new cars today-- by seven men and one woman, who, by the way, constantly make fun of each other in this raunchy way that we cannot play you over the radio. Just know that that's happening.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Plus, there are two guys in the finance department. And then, overseeing all of them, there are the general manager, Freddie, who you already met, and then, out on the showroom floor all day, every day, are two managers who you're going to be hearing from a lot over the course of this hour. These are Mike Perez and Sal Lanzilotta.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of the two, Sal is the more complicated figure. Balding, with a gray goatee, he's got this vibe that is halfway between Ben Kingsley in Gandhi and the laconic hitman Mike from Breaking Bad. When Sal gets up to speak at the weekly sales meetings-- the meeting, by the way, is in the middle of the showroom-- he paces around a red convertible as he talks, reminding everybody of the basic tenets of car sales.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: Customer says they're not ready to buy a car. They're all not ready to buy a car. Let's go over it again. They're in a car dealership.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: They got in their car, drove through hell to get here, looked for a parking spot for 10 minutes, parked, got out of the car, and walked into a car dealer. Not because the coffee's good. We went over this. Because the coffee here is not good. They came here because we sell cars, and they want to buy one.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nothing's changed in a hundred years of selling cars, he tells them at one meeting. The customer wants to pay as little as possible. We want to make as much as we can.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: You guys know the job, right? You've all done it before.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Be aggressive.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: Be aggressive. ABC, Bob. What's ABC?

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: Always Be Closing.

segments.speaker: Marc Brodlieb
segments.text: Always be closing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So these guys, the managers, Sal and Mike, sit near the front door of the showroom at this elevated platform that everybody calls the podium or the desk, and they oversee all the terms of all the deals.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And if you've ever bought a car, maybe you've wondered what really happens when the salesman leaves you and they go back and they talk to their manager, they talk to the boss. What do they do? Well, what they do is, we were told, they load their lips. Here's Freddie.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: We tell them what to say to the customer. And we load their lips, send it back to the customer, and see where we can commit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So for instance, when one of the salesmen wants to get a woman to bring her husband in today to test drive the car that she's chosen, they huddle at the desk, a bunch of them, and Freddie starts to improv some lines for the salesman to say.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Listen, if you can take this car by Monday, what happens-- if I can. I'm not sure if I can do it. I have money for the weekend that I'm giving away from Chrysler. As long as you purchase it by tomorrow and pick it up by Monday, you win.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He's totally making this up. There's no weekend money like this.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I've got extra money over the weekend through Chrysler. I want to use it. I want to give it to you. Get your husband in here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And with that, the salesman heads off.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: That's loading the lips. You've just seen it. Loading your lips.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But before the managers can load their lips, they have to figure out what price they're going to ask for and the terms of the deal and all that. And this works differently, I think, than the way that most of us imagine is happening when we buy a car. We assume that the managers and the salesmen are a unified team, and it's us versus them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But in fact, managers and salespeople are often at odds with each other, and they spin information and they lie to each other. Here's Peter Possas, a very experienced salesman, who, at the time of this recording, was three cars shy of the 18 that he was supposed to sell in October. And what he's doing here is he's asking a couple what they want their monthly payments to be on a new car.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: What if I can get you the same payment you're at now? $199 for 39 months, something like that?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, hear that? $199 a month. Then Peter marches over to talk to the managers at the desk. And listen to the number that he tells Sal that the customer wants.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: She wants it to be about $150 a month.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: $150. Not $199. As soon as Sal is out of earshot, Peter turns to the reporter who's trailing him, Sean Cole.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: You see what I did?

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So talk me through it.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: You heard-- well, you saw what-- she told me she wants to be at $199 a month.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: But I'm telling him $150 because I've got to work him, too, at the same time I'm working her.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: Oh, so you're going lower with him.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: I see.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why do this? Well, later, when the negotiations get tough, the manager, Sal, may ask Peter to squeeze the customers for a lower number on their trade-in, or maybe a higher price for the car, something that might be hard to talk the customer into. But Peter now has wiggle room. He knows he can push the couple up to $199 a month in payments because they already said yes to it. He can make up the difference there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In fact, as the deal proceeds, it runs into a problem. The desk, the couple, and the salesman cannot come to an agreement about how much the dealership should pay the couple for their trade-in. Sal says it is worth one price. The customers say that another Jeep dealer offered them a lot more than that for the trade-in. But of course, that may be a lie. There's a saying in the business-- buyers are liars. Or maybe the other dealership is lying to the customers. Maybe the other dealership told them an unrealistically high price that they never intend to pay. That happens, too. Everyone is playing everyone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sal, at the desk, tells Peter, the salesman, that the customer cannot be getting that trade-in price from the competitor. It can't be true.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: Stop believing what the customer's telling you. That car does $16,500 at the auction. There's no way they're paying him $20,000 grand on a car that they could sell at auction for $16,500.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: Then I guess he's a better negotiator than me.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: I think he's just a better liar, and you're buying it.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: That's the difference.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So to summarize, the managers and the salespeople are playing each other. The customer is playing them both. Each dealership is playing the other dealerships. And the manufacturer is playing all the dealerships, with its quotas and its incentives. Chrysler sold 140,083 cars and trucks in October. This is what it took to sell one of them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like I said earlier, several of us came and recorded at this dealership and each of us chose different salespeople to follow. Robyn Semien chose Bobby Tantillo. A warning to listeners, somebody uses a word in an offensive way in her story. We're going to leave that in because we're trying to document what really happened.

segments.text: Robert Tantillo-- Bobby T around the dealership-- is in last place. He doesn't like talking about it.

segments.text: How many cars have you sold?

segments.text: I didn't have to ask them. Freddie makes it clear in that weekly speech he gives every Saturday. Remember that meeting? He goes over everyone's individual sales, gives them new goals. Bob's there that morning, too. Freddie is keeping track.

segments.text: Bob T, you're at three. Thanks for stopping by.

segments.text: Bob doesn't flinch. He sits poker-faced in a chair. A couple of guys look down or stare at their hands.

segments.text: Bobby T's new here. Before this, he was in the wholesale food business for three decades, became a car salesman a few years ago after he retired. Bob says last month, he had the most sales for a couple weeks. But last month was last month. Freddie needs this month.

segments.text: Bob says the issue is, there's just so much about selling cars that's out of his control. He says his biggest problem this month is a lack of leads. One way salesmen get leads is from the internet. Town & Country lists all the cars it has online.

segments.speaker: Robyn Semien
segments.text: When people see one they like, they usually call before they come in to make sure the car is really there. But those calls go to guys in the back, in the internet department. Then when the customers show up at the store, they meet whoever they talk to on the phone, and one of the bosses at the desk hands them over to a real salesperson, like Bob. Except that Bob says he's never been handed one of those leads.

segments.text: They're going to give it to a guy that they know is-- that's been here. And they feed him the deal. That's pretty much how it works.

segments.text: Freddie raises his eyebrows at Bob and nods his head slowly like, you got that? Bob misunderstands the cue. segments.text: And I sent Bob T over there to get you or whatever and then come back. Where'd he go?

segments.text: He's like retarded. He's retarded.

segments.text: He didn't say, there's a customer here. Take care of the customer. He said, go get Dan. So I went and got Dan. I was supposed to know what he's thinking.

segments.text: You've got to be thick-skinned. You've got to be able to take a lot, absorb a lot. He said, well, now we gave it to the other guy. OK. What do you want me to say?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So there actually is a place at Town & Country where they keep score of who has sold what. It's in Freddie's office, the general manager's office. It's a whiteboard with each person's sales for the month to date on it. Every car or truck that they've sold is represented by a little magnetic rectangle that's roughly the size of a 9-volt battery. Everybody calls these chips. And the different colors of the chips stand for different models of cars and trucks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And throughout the day, salesmen come and they hover around the whiteboard, seeing where everybody stands. And generally, everybody is shooting for at least 15 sales a month. At 15 sales, your commission for the next month jumps from 20% to 30%.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's also a bonus of $600 when you hit 10 cars, $250 if you sell seven cars in the first two weeks of the month. There's money you get directly from Chrysler, and that could be anywhere between $50 and $250 per car. Mid-level salesmen here and Town & Country make around $60,000 a year. Top performers are closer to $100,000. Most of that is commissions and bonuses.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The number one salesman at Town & Country is always the same. Some months, he has twice as many sales as whoever's in second place.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: I've been doing this 28 years. This guy is one of the best I've ever seen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's salesman Peter Possas standing at the board. It's the middle of the month.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: He's got 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8-- 15, two pending. 17 cars. Unbelievable. This guy's a born salesperson.

segments.text: All the veteran sales guys at Town & Country say these things about this guy. He also happens to be the youngest salesman of dealership. He's 28. Jason Mascia. Reporter Sean Cole followed him around.

segments.text: Jason stands out from everybody else on the sales floor in pretty much every way. He's taller than everybody else and way more focused on his appearance-- always a full suit and tie, double Windsor knot, gelled hair. He's handsome. segments.text: So I'm going to go on my login here. And then, boom.

segments.text: Yeah, because I look at it and I say, that's freaking crazy. You know what I'm saying? You would think a guy that's in this business for 15 to 20 years should be doing that stuff.

segments.text: Jason's barely been in this business for four years. When I met him in the last weekend of October, he had already outsold everybody for the month, including a guy who's been doing this since Jason was a toddler. But he says he's not competing with the others. He's competing with himself.

segments.speaker: Jason Mascia
segments.text: I'm trying to excel. I have my own goals that nobody would even know about. You know what I mean? So I'm like my own little celebrity in my own little body.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: As we're sitting there talking, he pulls out a piece of paper and starts writing down everything he's saying as he says it. He always does this. I have 10 pages of notes from this interview-- his notes.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: So most of the salespeople at Town & Country are shooting for 15 to 20 sales in a month. That's considered a solid performance. And Jason is not satisfied with a solid performance.

segments.speaker: Jason Mascia
segments.text: There's a number that I really want to hit.

segments.speaker: Sean Cole
segments.text: He writes down that number and circles it and then moves on.

segments.speaker: Jason Mascia
segments.text: And I would love to just achieve-- I have achieved 30 cars several times.

segments.text: Nobody's giving you a runaround, Jessica, OK? Yelling and screaming and being rude and threatening is not going to get you anywhere. The car-- the car-- the car is a great car.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Next fight, he calls a woman in the back office who he thinks ratted to Freddie about a deal she didn't like.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: Theresa? Well, can you pick up the phone? Nails could get done later. Why did you run-- why did you run to Freddie? Why did you run to Freddie and tell Freddie about a Chrysler 300? Whose conversation? Why were you talking to Eddie? First of all, if a manager writes off on a deal and signs it-- she hung up the phone.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: I'm sort of surprised anyone would have the balls to fight with Joe. He's a big man-- 350 pounds. Large and in charge. The day I meet him, he's wearing a gray tracksuit,

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: but what I quickly find out is that he's wearing a tracksuit because it's his day off. He's supposed to be at his son Mike's football game against Malvern. He hasn't been able to catch an away game all season, and he took this one Sunday off to do it. It was important to him.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: For so many years, he wasn't around enough for his kids. He's working all the time. Joe knows Mike will be looking for him in the stands right about now. And he's not going to be there because he's here at the car lot.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: We're a little shorthanded, so I've got to be here, which is not a problem. Listen, if I'm making money, I'm making money. Just it's a catch-22. You're missing a game, but that's the car business.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: That's the car business. I'll make it up to him later.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Yesterday, Joe was late to his mother-in-law's surprise 70th birthday party. And last week, he was late for his own mother's 60th. The used car side of Town & Country is supposed to sell 70 cars by the end of the month. That's Joe's version of the 129 on the new side.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: When I first met Joe, used was at 35. At stake is Joe's big year-end bonus. Joe wouldn't tell me the amount of the bonus, but he made it clear it's very, very nice. Down-payment-on-a-house nice.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Since he fell so behind the last couple months, this month, October, is make or break for Joe. He's got to get to at least 70 cars if he wants any hope of reaching that bonus by the end of the year. And it's not looking good. 20 years in the business, Joe's never seen a stretch this slow for this long.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Joe blames it mostly on Hurricane Sandy. A year ago, tens of thousands of people lost their cars all at once. And they got new ones all at once. So now, a year later, tens of thousands of people are out of the used car market who normally would be buying and selling right now.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: We had two weekends in a row we sold one car.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: For two Saturdays and two Sundays, and we sold one car.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: In the whole weekend?

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: The whole weekend. The whole two weekends, we sold one car. There was days we didn't see a customer.

segments.speaker: Sarah      Koenig
segments.text: Joe goes outside to do an appraisal on a Nissan Quest. This also gives him a chance to have a cigarette, one of about 40 Parliaments he'll smoke today. His wife and kids get on him about the smoking. He's got six kids. Six kids-- two are grown, four of them still at home.

segments.speaker: Sarah      Koenig
segments.text: Joe's the only breadwinner in the family-- always has been-- so it's all on him. Even in the best of times, Joe's a worrier, like his grandmother. He's 42 years old, but he looks older. In the past year, he's gained about 80 pounds.

segments.speaker: Sarah      Koenig
segments.text: In the parking lot, Joe throws away a half-smoked cigarette and then looks over the Nissan Quest. Tires are so-so. Needs some detailing. It's got a cracked taillight and a bad CARFAX report, meaning it's been in an accident. $2,000 is fair for this car, Joe says. It's what these are going for at auction.

segments.speaker: Sarah      Koenig
segments.text: He tells me the customers are going to want at least $2,500, but there's no way he can do that. $2,500 is just too much. He heads back inside.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: $2,500, that's everything.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Instantly caves.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: That's what I will do.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: He needs the deal. They shake on it.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Joe was about 22 when he started in the car business. He had a baby at 18-- his son, Joseph-- and then four more kids-- Dean, Chris, Michael, and Adriana, plus his stepson, Louis.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Joe himself was one of five kids. His mom raised them by herself, no dad around, no money. He moved around a lot. With his own kids, he's the uptight parent, the one who doesn't laugh enough, the one who hammers them about consequences. He wants his kids to fear his wrath but also to know he loves them. Sometimes, it's tricky for him to balance that or even to talk about it.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: I have a good relationship with my children. I didn't have a father. So it's hard to do something when you don't know how to do it. Sometimes you don't know how to do-- I'm like a manly man.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: So I love them very much, but I don't know how to sometimes show it to them. I kiss them. I hug them. But you know what I'm saying? Something that I have to adapt to. But that's it. They're good. They're good kids.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Joe wants his kids to have more stability than he had growing up and a better standard of living. For 16 years, they all lived in a big house in Smithtown in a fairly wealthy neighborhood. And Joe says there was pressure there. Some other kids at school had fancy clothes and extravagant vacations, blow-out sweet 16 parties. He didn't want his kids to feel less-than, so he made sure, within reason, that they had what the other kids had.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But three years ago, he left Town & Country for another job at a Toyota dealer, and it didn't go well at all. He lost-- well, he says he lost everything. But in any case, it was a lot of money. They sold their big house in Smithtown and moved to a smaller house in Levittown, about five minutes from the dealership. And in a lot of ways, Joe's glad about that. It's made them closer as a family, he says.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: But he's also trying to work his way back up. He'd like to be able to buy them all a bigger house, give everyone a little more room. That's why he's so worried about this bad stretch of business and about getting that bonus.

segments.speaker: Sarah Koenig
segments.text: Toward the end of the day, his son Mike calls. Joe's already spoken to the coach about how the football game went.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: Two sacks and two tackles. That's great.

segments.speaker: Mike Monti
segments.text: OK. Wait, Dad.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Mike Monti
segments.text: Do you think [INAUDIBLE] to your job so you can give us some money so we can go get something to eat?

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: Yeah. All right. I'll be home in probably, hopefully, like 20 minutes, and I'll give you money to go out to eat.

segments.speaker: Mike Monti
segments.text: OK. [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: All right. Bye.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: Every one of them. And it's hard to say no. You try your best. When you're doing well, it's no big deal, and you can take care of them. And then there's just doing well to where you're making it by.

segments.speaker: Joe Monti
segments.text: What is it? Today's October. What's going to happen in a couple of months when my son's get ready to leave for college? Am I going to have the money?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's mid-afternoon on the new car side of Town & Country. So what do you do all day on the last day of the month when you need to sell everything you possibly can? Well, instead of waiting for customers to come into the store, you call up any lead you have and try to close deals right over the phone if you can.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the salespeople, Lori, does this with a previous customer. Jason also sells to a guy he knows over the phone. Peter gets a lead from a cop upstate that he sold a Durango truck to. The lead is a friend of the cop's, also a cop, who wants the same deal his friend got. Peter gets him on the phone and says he'll give him the deal for two reasons.

segments.speaker: Peter Possas
segments.text: One of them, you were referred. And the other one is you're an officer of the law, and we respect that over here, big time, just so you know.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, this leaves out the third and main reason for the great deal that he's getting-- they need eight more sales by 9 o'clock. And the cop ends up buying his Durango for $2,214 less than the dealership paid for it. Even after finance charges and holdback and all the other ways they make money, they still lost on this one.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Ditto this guy, Richard Massana. He was going to get an oil change this morning and stepped in on a whim and they showed him numbers way lower than any other dealer that he'd been to. Richard called up his wife to let her know, hey, surprise, we're getting a new truck. On his test drive, he still seemed amazed at what was happening.

segments.speaker: Richard Massana
segments.text: Who would have thought Halloween, buying a truck? I never thought it would happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: His payment will be $425 a month. The salesman says later that it should have been $525, but it's the end of the month. Turns out, yes, it is true that you do get a better deal at the end of the month at Town & Country-- at least any month that they're struggling to make their goal.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When you actually look at the numbers, the cars that they sell on the last two days, the average deal actually loses money versus the deals that they make at the beginning of the month, where they made about $900 per car. OK, for car people, I'm now going to say these words. I am factoring in everything they made on financing and warranties and extras and holdback and the 1% they get from Chrysler on every car when I make that statement.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I am not factoring in any money that they would get if they hit their number and get their bonus from Chrysler. That would add about $500 per car, which still does not give them a huge profit per car. It used to be a lot higher. But today, because people research prices on the internet, profit margins on new cars are lower than what they used to be, not just here at this dealership, but everywhere in the car business.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The owner of Town & Country told me that he used to make $500 more per car, and each salesman made more per car. Now they all have to make it up in volume. So it's more of a grind, a harder job with tighter deals and less reward.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And if you're wondering, car dealerships make less profit than other businesses. A recent study by an outfit called Sageworks found that car dealers end up with less than $0.03 on every dollar they make as profit, which is less profit than furniture stores, office supply stores, restaurants. Lower than pretty much everything but grocery stores. When car dealers say that they are not making a killing, on average, it's true.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At some point during this last day of the month, one of the deals that they had been counting on falls through. Mike Lester's sale of a red Grand Cherokee. But turns out that's no problem for the dealership because Scott has a customer who wants that exact same truck. You remember that deal the day before, where two salesmen sold the same car to two different customers. The mortician? It's that salesman and that customer, and the salesman, Scott, is very, very happy. And the only bad news about all of this is what it does to Mike Lester's sales total for the month.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: That drops me down to 14.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: 14 sucks because, like I said earlier, 15 is the magic number. 15 is where the serious bonuses and commissions kick in. Most of the guys count on getting those.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: It could add up to big money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But then, Scott, whose customer is now going to get the red Grand Cherokee, Scott realizes what this means for Mike and says to Mike--

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: Wait, is that your 15th car?

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: You take the chip. Give him the chip. Switch it around.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: And split it with me.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now Mike will get the credit for the sale. He's at 15 again.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: OK, yeah. Love you, Scott.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Scott kisses Mike on the cheek. Producer Brian Reed witnesses all this.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So you're at 15 now?

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Did he owe you one, or?

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: No, but we always help each other out, especially on the last day of the month.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: How do you feel?

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: Excited.

segments.speaker: Mike Lester
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So amidst anxious salesmen and salesmen literally running to the desk or to finance, there is one salesman who is a model of calm. Even his cubicle is different from everybody else's. There's no swag. There's no pictures of family. There are no good luck charms. It's bare. The salesman, his name is Manny Rosales, says he doesn't like the distractions. One of our producers, Brian, who you just heard, got to know him.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Manny is 58, born in Peru. He has gray hair and glasses. One morning at the showroom, he gestured cryptically for me to come over to his desk, as if he had a secret to tell me. Turn that off, he said, pointing to my tape recorder.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I explained that I was a radio reporter and I needed to record whatever he was going to tell me for it to be useful, but he wasn't having it. He seemed unimpressed by our little radio story. He said my colleagues and I were like fishermen who had no idea what we were angling for. We had no focus. We were just casting blindly.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Manny, I soon learned, is a man of many metaphors. I put down my recorder. The thing you need to be paying attention to, he said, is the negotiation. The salesman is the tiger, and the customer is the deer.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: The tiger has to eat, and you can't eat if you don't kill that deer. He moved his right hand up and then clamped his fingers around his own neck. You have to go for the neck, he said. But if you try to kill him too early, the deer will wake up and run away.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: As the day went on, I kept trying to get Manny to let me record him, but he wouldn't. Instead, he'd come up to me while I was interviewing someone else, point to his head very deliberately, presumably to his brain, give me a knowing look, and then walk away. At one point, we found ourselves facing each other at his desk. He asked me if I had read the greatest book ever written about car sales. I don't think so, I told him. What is it? The Art of War, he said, by Sun Tzu.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Sun Tzu, as you maybe know, was a military general and strategist in ancient China. The Art of War is his magnum opus, where he lays out his tactics for how to succeed in conflict. And though Sun Tzu was writing about actual war, the book has become well known in business and sales circles. It's kind of like The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People, if that had been written in the fifth century BC on individual strips of bamboo.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So I went to the bookstore and bought a copy and then headed back to Town & Country.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Manny, how are you, sir? Can I show you the homework I've been doing?

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: Please.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I handed him my copy of The Art of War, which I'd marked up with notes about its relevance to car sales. I could see why Manny felt that it spoke to his profession. Lines like, "draw them in with the prospect of gain," "take them by confusion" seemed especially on point.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: How far are you?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: I finished it.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: You finished it? OK. I want to ask you a question. What have you learned?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What have I learned? Well, I'm here to learn some more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I was in. For two days, Manny took me under his wing with my recorder running and became my sales sensei.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Manny's kind of an unusual car salesman because he has no affection for cars at all. If a customer asks him how much horsepower a car has or how quickly it can go from 0 to 60, usually he has to look up the answer or go ask a coworker. He has no interest in that stuff. So instead, Manny developed a way to sell the customer using a different approach.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: The psychology. How you penetrate his brain.

segments.speaker: Film Narrator
segments.text: Sun Tzu says all warfare is deception.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: To help me understand this-- how to penetrate the brain of one's opponent-- Manny showed me a couple of movies on YouTube. One was a re-enactment of the Second Punic War in the third century BC, Hannibal's campaign against the Romans. Manny wanted me to pay attention to one battle in particular from that war, the Battle of Cannae.

segments.speaker: Film Narrator
segments.text: One of the bloodiest ever fought.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: At Cannae, Hannibal's troops were vastly outnumbered. He had about 40,000 men versus Rome's army, which had roughly 85,000.

segments.speaker: Hannibal
segments.text: The Romans will have the confidence that comes only with greater numbers. We'll present them with the unexpected and watch them fall apart.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: See, that is the secret. Present the unexpected.

segments.speaker: Hannibal
segments.text: Our forces will be arranged like this.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: The details of Hannibal's strategy are a bit complicated to go into here. Manny had to draw me a diagram to help me get it. But let's just say it involves an unusual troop formation that made the Romans think they were gaining ground when really they were at Hannibal's whim.

segments.speaker: Hannibal
segments.text: At this point, the Romans will think they have won. Let them taste victory.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: We're watching this, remember, on a laptop on the showroom floor. Customers are milling about, checking out the new cars, as Hannibal's mercenaries and cavalry encircle the Romans and trap them for good.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: [BATTLE SOUNDS]

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: And now the killing has started.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: [BATTLE SOUNDS CONTINUE]

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So how does Manny use this to sell Dodge Chargers? Well, just like Hannibal would, he presents the customer with the unexpected.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What they expect is for the salesman to be pushy and try to coerce them into buying a car at a certain price. So Manny does the opposite. He acts as if he doesn't even want to sell the car. He agrees with the customer, uses a similar tone, repeats words the customer says. If someone comes in and says he's just there to browse, not to buy, that's totally fine, Manny will say, and he'll back off.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: The idea is to make them believe that he's doing everything from his point of view. So he's thinking he's playing his game.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: But he's really not?

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: Absolutely not.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: What game is he playing in reality?

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: My game. Simple. Simple.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Manny gave me an example of this that he'd executed a few days earlier with a customer named Julio, who was looking for a Jeep Grand Cherokee. Julio runs warehouses for a living and negotiates for his company, so Manny knew he'd be a formidable opponent. Julio told me later that he'd already visited seven other Jeep dealerships by the time he got to Town & Country and was calling and texting with another three.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: When he sat down across from Manny, Julio made the first offer, $36,000. The Jeep was listed at $45,000, so Julio's offer was absurdly low. Julio knew it was unrealistic. He expected Manny to say no way, that he could never give it to him for that price.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: But then listen to what Manny did instead.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: I said, all right. If I can sell it to you for $36,000, are you ready to do it right now? Show me the money. Where's the credit card?

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Where's the credit card. Manny says this was the key move, the unexpected move.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: Because they never thought I would say yes. Suddenly, they don't know what to do or what to say. They get confused. He cannot back up because that's what he said to me. If you give me $36,000, I'll buy the car.

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: [BATTLE SOUNDS]

segments.speaker: Hannibal
segments.text: At this point, the Romans will think they have won. Let them taste victory.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So he pulled his credit card out?

segments.speaker: Manny Rosales
segments.text: Absolutely. He gave it to me. And I said, all right, let me take the offer to my manager, even though I knew that we cannot do it.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: After days of negotiation, Manny ended up scoring this deal. Julio paid $40,000 for the Jeep, which was low. The dealership lost money on the car. But after it was all over, Julio told me that this move, when Manny pretended to take his low offer seriously, he said, without that, he would have walked out of Town & Country immediately, which would have meant no sale, nothing towards the monthly quota.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: By 4:00 PM, the hustling in the showroom is paying off. Chips are going up on the board in Freddie's office. Even one of the guys in the back rooms is pitching in-- a finance guy, Terrance Kelly, TK. He's reaching for the phone.

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: So basically, the numbers are down. They need all the deals. So they made me call my niece in Las Vegas, believe it or not. She's been trying to buy a car anyway.

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Katie
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: Hi, Katie.

segments.speaker: Katie
segments.text: Hey.

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: How are you? I have you on the speakerphone.

segments.speaker: Katie
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: TK's got 34 nieces and nephews. Katie is his goddaughter, though, so he keeps a special eye out for her. At the time that this was recorded, the rest of the family didn't know that she was pregnant, though he did. Even though he did not know, until he picked up the receiver and started filling out the forms for the car sale, her fiance's last name.

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: OK. Charles Parker? You're getting married to somebody with the last name of Parker? Oh, Barker. Oh. Is he related to Bob at all?

segments.speaker: Terrance Kelly
segments.text: What does he do, by the way? I never asked you. Ooh. HVAC company? Nice. I like that. Well, as long as he's happy. You're in the right area for air conditioning, I guess.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The dealership is selling the car to Katie below cost at a $900 loss. And TK is going to end up spending $1,200 of his own money to ship the car out to her in Las Vegas. And this? This is the sale that puts him over the top. This is the 129th sale of the month.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just a few minutes before 5 o'clock, right after this happens, I stop by Freddie the general manager's office. Nobody is running into high fives. There's not even a staff announcement on the PA saying they made it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I've got to say, it's weirdly anticlimactic.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: There's no hurrah. There's no balloons falling from the ceiling. We did our job. Everybody earned their paycheck. That's the bottom line.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then the clock starts ticking tomorrow morning on next month?

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: We're all a bunch of losers tomorrow morning. You start all over again. That's how it goes. Oh, the wife. Oh, my god. Don't get married.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: We're fighting because I told-- she says to me, what time are you getting home? I said, what time do I usually get home at the end of the month? Whenever I get home. What, do you want a time card? What, am I in punching in?

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I said, when I get home, I get home, and I hung up on her. So now she's pissed and she's texting. "OK, so why do you have to bite my head off?" I told her she should've married a plumber. 9:00 to 5:00, OK? Weekends off, OK?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He texts her back. This fight actually continues for the next few hours over text message. Then, at 6:57, two hours before closing, one of the managers, Mike Perez, and Jason start huddling the desk, a little freaked out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mike walks to Freddie's office to explain the problem to Freddie. Their count is wrong. They're not at 129 because there's an extra chip on the board.

segments.speaker: Mike Perez
segments.text: There was a chip up here that was supposed to be pulled off.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: What do you mean? We're down one?

segments.speaker: Mike Perez
segments.text: Yeah. This was up there. It should have been off of there because the customer switched cars. But someone put the new chip up but didn't take the old chip off.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: So I'm still at 128?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Freddie does know that, at this moment, there is another deal being negotiated that could possibly get them back up to 129. Peter is the salesman for that one. But the deal is stuck over the price of the customer's trade-in, what they should pay for it.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Go make that deal right now. Whatever it is, just make the fucking deal.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But that deal is not too easy to settle. And while they're waiting, more bad news. You remember that red Grand Cherokee that Scott and Mike Lester each had sold to different people and then Mike Lester's guy dropped out and Scott got the deal, and there was the kiss? Now Scott's guy also drops out. He doesn't want to buy tonight because he wants his mom to see the car tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Freddie overhears Scott saying this to one of the managers.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: What, you have a problem? What's the matter with it? What's the matter with it, Scotty?

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: The guy wants to show his mom tomorrow the car. Originally--

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: What do you mean? This isn't a deal?

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: I thought it was, but--

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Are you fucking kidding me? You have insurance on this car and everything?

segments.speaker: Scott Froehlich
segments.text: I don't even-- he didn't even send it into the bank because we don't have his prior employer.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: What are we doing? I thought these all went into the bank today! I asked you, all the cars have insurance and went into the bank? You've got to be fucking kidding me!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Scott's deal is dead. They're at 127 with just two hours left before closing.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: I'm fucked. I just lost Scott's. I'm fucked.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So now they scramble to figure out, OK, there was Mike Lester's customer for that red Grand Cherokee. Could they possibly give him better terms that would bring him back to the table? Freddie orders one of the managers, Mike Perez, to make that happen.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Just do it. It's going to be too late. You're going to wait a half hour longer. It's getting later and later. I'd rather have a sure thing than not. Just fucking do it. How much does that lose?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. The only question is, how much does the deal lose, not whether it loses. So Mike Perez calls Richie in finance. Richie tells him he's in luck. The guy actually called back saying that he would agree to the terms but-- OK, here's the catch-- he just wants 24 hours to think about this. Mike Perez asks, OK, if we sweeten the terms, can we get him to decide right now? Rich doesn't think so.

segments.speaker: Rich
segments.text: It's not going to change anything tonight. For me to pull down my pants, you don't need to.

segments.speaker: Mike Perez
segments.text: But Freddie's telling me to. Literally, he's telling me to, so I need to just--

segments.speaker: Rich
segments.text: Bro, whatever you need to do. But I'm telling you, if I told him it was free and the same, you're going to get the same answer anyway-- 24 hours.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All is lost.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then, in just six minutes, they turn it around. Rich offers a better deal to that guy on the red Grand Cherokee after all and yes, he takes it. And Peter's deal that was stuck over the price of the trade-in gets unstuck when the managers suck it up and pay $1,500 more for the trade-in than they think it's worth. Back to 129.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Everybody seems a little stunned by what just happened when it's done. Freddie and Sal look out at the showroom from the desk like old sailors on the deck of a 19th century ship that just got thrashed around by a hurricane and also a murderous white whale.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Do you believe this shit, Sal? I feel like back in fucking Infiniti days.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: This is ridiculous, this month.

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: This is just--

segments.speaker: Sal Lanzilotta
segments.text: The month wasn't bad enough. We've got to suffer a little more the last day of the month.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: Un-fucking-believable. Fuck me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Freddie's phone, of course, doesn't stop with the text messages through all this.

segments.speaker: Freddie Hoyt
segments.text: [SIGHS] God damn. The wife, who else? I don't know what she's even fighting for.

segments.speaker: Ira      Glass
segments.text: They get their bonus from Chrysler, $68,000. And because of it, the dealership ends up in the black, not the red, for the month. Jason finishes the month at 29 cars, almost twice anyone else, as usual. Manny has 10; Mike L, 15; Scott, 18.

segments.speaker: Ira      Glass
segments.text: The used car side, Joe Monti's side, did not meet its goal. They were hoping for 70. They got 57, meaning Joe Monti probably will not be getting his year-end bonus this year.

segments.speaker: Ira      Glass
segments.text: And Bob T, the salesman at the bottom of the board with the least sales this month, well, the night isn't over for Bob T.

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: Where'd you put the key? Where'd you put the car? I've got the key. Where's the car?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not long after they reached 129, a couple walks in wanting to buy a Dodge Dart for their 19-year-old son. Bob T rushes them through the test drive, has the husband sit at his computer and use his phone to quickly call the insurance company and then runs-- literally runs-- to get their new car prepped and inspected in the garage.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Bob, is this one going tonight?

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: He says to bring it right over to service.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, but is it going, or is it a paper delivery?

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: I don't know if it's going.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Find out.

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: It should go.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Who the fuck wants to take a car home at 10 o'clock at night? You still got the receipt for them? Bring them back!

segments.speaker: Bob Tantillo
segments.text: These guys could say what they want. This old timer, nobody works as fast as me here. You notice that? Huh? Yes or no?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And with that, Bob T lands Town & Country's last sale of the month, number 130, one car past the goal of 129. Or anyway, that's what they thought that night. The next morning, when everybody comes in, they look at Chrysler's official count on the computer. And according to Chrysler, no, their count was wrong. One of their sales should not have been counted in October, which means that they did not have 130 cars like they thought. They had only 129, exactly 129. Which means, yes, it was Bob T and his very last sale of the month that took them across the finish line. Bob T saved the day.
